Elicit

AI research assistant for systematic literature review.

What is Elicit?

AI research assistant for systematic literature review. Searches a corpus of ~125 million academic papers, extracts structured data from each into a comparison table, and summarises findings across studies.

Best for

Systematic reviews and structured evidence extraction at scale.

Main features

  • Semantic paper search across ~125M papers
  • automatic data extraction into custom table columns
  • systematic review workflow
  • screening with custom inclusion criteria
  • Elicit Reports
  • PDF upload and extraction
  • citation export
  • notebook for multi-step research.

Practical use cases

  • Running a systematic literature review
  • screening hundreds of abstracts against inclusion criteria
  • extracting sample sizes, methods and outcomes into a structured table
  • finding papers on a concept rather than a keyword.

Who is it for?

  • Academic researchers, PhD students, systematic reviewers, evidence-synthesis teams, pharma and biotech research, policy analysts.

Pricing, free access & limits

Freemium with credit-based extraction; per-seat team and enterprise plans

Plans described in the source

Basic free with a monthly credit allowance. Plus around $12/mo billed annually (about $15 monthly) with a larger credit pool and unlimited search. Pro around $49/mo annually for high-volume extraction and reports. Team and Enterprise priced per seat on request. Credits are consumed per paper column extracted.

Free plan

Yes - Basic free plan with unlimited search and a limited monthly credit allowance for extraction.

Free trial

Free plan serves as the trial; institutional pilots arranged through sales.

Usage limits to consider

Credit-metered: each cell of extracted data from each paper consumes credits, so a 200-paper, 8-column extraction is expensive. Free tier credits are quickly exhausted by any real review.

Strengths & tradeoffs

These points summarize the supplied research, rather than hands-on test results.

Strengths noted in the source

  • Purpose-built for systematic review rather than generic chat
  • extraction into structured tables is a real time-saver
  • grounded strictly in the paper corpus so hallucination risk is lower
  • transparent about which paper each claim came from.

Limitations to consider

  • Corpus skews heavily toward English-language and open-access literature
  • paywalled full texts often unavailable so extraction works from abstracts
  • credit pricing makes large reviews costly
  • extraction accuracy still requires human verification for publication-grade work.

Platforms, languages & integrations

Platforms

  • Web (browser only)

Languages

  • Interface English; indexed literature is predominantly English

API access

Enterprise API available on request

Integrations and exports

  • Zotero, BibTeX/RIS citation export, CSV export, PDF upload

Evaluation notes

Always spot-check extracted values against the source PDF - accuracy is good but not publication-grade unverified. Budget credits against the number of papers multiplied by the number of columns, not by seats.
